What film is this $10,000 for?
Is my hon. friend asking about the reduction in the film vote?

I wanted to know what films
were being made this year, and whether the work was being done by the national film board or a commercial company.

Any films we have made are
produced by the national film board.

In the details at page 270 I see an item of $50,000 for advertising in Canada and abroad, as compared with $95,000 for last year. Then there is $35,000 for booklets, an increase of $10,000 over last year. There is $10,000 for films, to which the hon. member for Peterborough West referred, as compared with $30,000 last year. But in the first item of general administration there is an amount of $40,000 for trade promotion at home and abroad. What was the reason for transferring that $40,000 from publicity and advertising to administration?

The first item represents the
cost of looking after groups from abroad who come here to promote trade. It is not an advertising expense; it is what might be called a hospitality expense. The second item is an advertising expense, and there is a reduction this year. We thought that with the advertising that went on in connection with the trade fair we could afford to reduce the ordinary departmental advertising, and we have planned accordingly.
Does that $40,000 under the administrative item have anything to do with trade fair advertising?

No. The advertising item we
are now considering is for departmental advertising, in connection with any matters the department believes should be drawn to the attention of the public, such as changes in regulations and so on. The promotion of trade item is not an advertising item.

I do not think the minister
quite understood my question.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

I cannot hear you, for one
thing.

On page 270 there is a
reduction of $45,000 under advertising in Canada and abroad, as compared with last year. I asked the minister the reason for that reduction, and whether it was accounted for by the $40,000 under administration.

No, the two items are not related. The $40,000 item covers such things as the cost of the trip to the United Kingdom by the deputy minister, trade commissions abroad, tariff expeditions abroad and so on. The other is for advertising in publications and newspapers. There is a reduction in the latter item, which, as I have said, is made possible by the advertising incidental to the trade fair, which was paid for by the trade fair and which we think warrants a cut in the usual advertising appropriation.

Then there is a reduction of $20,000 in connection with films. Is that because the minister feels films are not doing the job, or perhaps because more films were made last year? What films were made last year for the $30,000, and what are proposed this year for the $10,000?

This is not to pay for the making of films. It is for making the sound tracks in foreign languages; and for distributing films made by the film board or other agencies of government. The distribution of films on trade matters is undertaken by the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Then this is not to pay for the production of films, but for transporting them around the' country?
This is the cost of translating them into foreign languages and preparing them for distribution in foreign countries.
Where your trade commissioners distribute them?
Yes.
Who paid for the films?

They have been paid for. Some of those produced in the past may have been paid for by the Department of Trade and Commerce. Others have been paid for by the national film board. They are out of the library of government films, chosen because they, have some significance in the country to which we send them.

An item slipped by while I was out, and I wanted to ask the minister just one question without enlarging upon it. I am told by a prominent agriculturist in this country that there is a large market awaiting Canadian butter in Venezuela. I wonder if
the minister has any information on that, or whether his department has made any recent investigation into the possibilities. If that were so it would be a great, boon to butter producers here, who are faced with pretty heavy competition and the prospect of rather low prices in some instances.

Mr. Chairman, we have moved butter to Venezuela, and we hope to move more. Our prices are somewhat out of line with those competing in the market, but I assure my hon. friend we shall lose no opportunity to sell butter in Venezuela.

Item agreed to.
General administration-
427.	Economic research and development branch, including the conducting of investigations and reporting upon commercial relations and foreign tariffs, and the development of Canadian industry, and a contribution of $6,300 to the International Customs Tariffs Bureau, $442,480.

Will the
minister add a word to what he said this afternoon on the question of the relationship between the tariff board and the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with the whole question of commercial relations and foreign tariffs. The minister did mention it this afternoon, but I was not too clear on the division. On the face of it, it looks as if there might be a duplication. I should like to have it explained to me.

Mr. Chairman, the tariff board acts as adviser to the Minister of Finance regarding domestic tariffs, that is tariffs placed on goods entering Canada. The branch we are discussing, the economic research branch, commercial relations division, deals with tariffs applied by foreign countries against Canadian goods. I think that is the distinction. There is no overlapping.

It is two
sides of the same coin, so to speak. The minister did say this afternoon that the very able head of the tariff board does take full part in trade discussions. Perhaps there is nothing more that need be said about it, but surely the subject does not divide itself sharply into two unrelated parts, foreign tariffs and domestic tariffs. They seem to be part of one problem.

We endeavour to make it one problem. The officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce interpret foreign tariffs to Canadian business, and obtain the views of Canadian business on foreign tariffs. This department takes a leading part in any discussion of foreign tariffs, such as have been current in recent years at Geneva and Annecy.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the United States tariff commission is now taking evidence about the importation of Canadian potatoes into the United States, which evidence is to be presented at Torquay this autumn. Will the minister state whether we shall have a representative at Torquay who will be posted concerning the importation of fruits and vegetables from the United States, so that he can present an argument against shutting out potatoes going to the United States?

Mr. Chairman, the tariff commission of the United States is taking evidence in the United States, and our trade officials are taking evidence in Canada. The hon. member will appreciate that a meeting such as Torquay is a meeting for trading. We expect that our delegation will be able to hold their own against the American delegation in discussing the tariff on potatoes entering the United States. In any case, we are endeavouring to see that they are as well prepared as possible.
While I am on my feet permit me to present my hon. friend with an up-to-date list of articles that can and cannot be imported into Canada. This is not a list prepared by the government, but a list prepared by the Cahadian Manufacturers Association. I will send it across to my hon. friend.

I shall be glad to have that list, and at the same time I should like to draw to the minister's attention a case concerning a manufacturer in the United States who built a plant at Montreal. He arranged to bring supplies from his plant in the United States to Montreal, thinking he could bring them in without any restriction. He found he was unable to do so, so last Wednesday he called me to see if I could help him. He is a competitor of mine, but I told him I would give him what help I could. We went to see the officials, and the first man we approached told us he would give this man a permit for enough supplies to last him two months, after which time he could get supplies in Canada. That was on Wednesday, June 21. On June 22, this official wrote a letter to the manufacturer at Lachine informing him that he could not bring in the supplies. The plant was ready to commence operations, and there were about fifty employees hired. This official, after telling his stenographer to send the permit to Rock Island so that it would be there in time for the goods to leave, wrote a letter stating that the chief officials of the board had turned down his 'application.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
This morning I took up the question again, and the official told me he was still ready to allow the goods to enter. I cannot understand why he wrote the letter of June 22.
May I ask the hon. member if the man to whom he refers is an officer of the Department of Trade and Commerce?
The matter has to do with trade and commerce, but the official is the assistant to the deputy minister of finance.
The hon. member is asking me a question about matters of which I have no knowledge.
It concerns import control.

Could the minister tell us something of the results obtained so far by the committee under the chairmanship of Mr. James Duncan, of the Massey-Harris Company, Toronto, which was set up some time ago to promote better trade relations between Great Britain and this country?

I would point out that the committee of which Mr. Duncan is chairman is a businessmen's committee set up by private enterprise. From my knowledge of its work, I can say it is obtaining excellent results. I believe the comparative trade figures for 1950 and 1949 would indicate that. Someone at least has brought about a great improvement, and I give full credit to the Duncan committee.

While we are discussing this matter of tariffs, I should like to mention again a matter I mentioned earlier. I see by the press that we are about to negotiate with the United States concerning tariffs. There is one industry that has been nearly ruined by taxation and tariffs, and that is the fur industry. I might say that the United States is the only country that puts up an excessive barrier against silver fox furs. Today the tariff is 37J per cent ad valorem. If the minister is to negotiate for lower tariffs or new concessions, I believe this is one matter that should be brought to his attention. While we allow furs from the United States to enter Canada duty free, the United States imposes a 37 J per cent ad valorem duty. At one time it was up to 50 per cent, but it was reduced a little. I should like the minister to make a note of that, and have his officials discuss it with the United States customs officers.

Mr. Chairman, industry across Canada has been invited to send in briefs covering any tariff reductions they hope to get. Those briefs are being studied. I have not the position of the fur industry in mind, but I shall take note of my friend's suggestion and look into it at the first opportunity.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

In that connection, Mr. Chairman, what is the effect on Canada of the cancellation of the reciprocal agreement between the United States and Mexico? Apparently we are likely to lose some trade because we can no longer get benefit by reason of the favoured nation clause.

It affects Canada indirectly. The United States have denounced their reciprocal trade arrangement-that is, their trade arrangement with Mexico-for the reason that they assert that Mexico has discriminated against Canadian trade.
Against American trade, you mean; you said Canadian trade.

Against American trade, yes. It will have a repercussion on Canada with regard to two items of which Mexico is the principal supplier. One is lead and the other is cattle. The items are down for discussion at Torquay in September and it is hoped that the Canadian position can be corrected at that time. If he asks me what items will be affected as a result of the action taken by the United States, those are the two principal items that will affect Canada.
Will the effect on lead be quite considerable?
It restores the duty. The present duty of one and a half cents a pound will go to three cents a pound.
Is that considered serious?
It is quite a bit.
What about oil? Is that not affected also?
It might affect our position if we were an exporter of oil, but we are not, so our position is not affected.

One other question I should like to ask on this item has to do with the lumber trade between the Pacific coast and Great Britain. Apparently the British are buying less and less lumber all the time. Within the last two weeks they have called for tenders on another order which is for only 200 million board feet, to be shared between the west coast states and British Columbia. Apparently British Columbia this year has sold to the United Kingdom 167 million board feet, and they will be sharing with Washington and Oregon in this new order for 200 million board feet; whereas in 1949 British Columbia sold a total of 345 million board feet and in 1939 sold practically one billion board feet. What is the position with regard to that trade? Is Russia cutting in? Is it likely to continue small or what are the prospects?

As I have stated before, Mr. Chairman, the trade cannot sell Canadian exports twice. The Canadian exports have been going to the United States, attracted there by the abnormally high prices. Prices today are much higher than prices at any other time since the war. My. hon. friend mentioned 2 million board feet.
Two hundred million board feet.	.

Yes, 200 million board feet. As I understand it, it is 2,000 standards, which is 400 million board feet. I think British Columbia can have all that order if they will quote a reasonable price. I do not think they can expect to get the American price; but they can certainly have it if they quote anything like the price which they applied to earlier exports to the United Kingdom.
Is not the purchase price of that lumber to be paid out of ECA funds?
Yes.

Under those circumstances it
would be unlikely that British Columbia would get the whole order, would it not?

British Columbia could have
had all the previous orders. They actually took only 75 per cent but they could have had it all had they been able to handle it. They only quoted on part of it. If British Columbia quotes on all this order and quotes a reasonable price, there is no doubt in the world but that all of the order will be placed in British Columbia.

Is Russian lumber cutting in
on the British market?

Russia has always had a good
share of the British market. I think its proportionate share at the moment is less than in the pre-war years; but it is shipping some lumber into the British market.

I understood the minister to say a moment or two ago that this denunciation of the trade treaty between the United States and Mexico might affect the tariff on Canadian cattle. Am I right in thinking that one of the few results that we got after the Geneva discussion of 1947 was a reduction in the tariff on cattle? I thought that was a definite bargain which would not be affected by anything else.

The Geneva agreements covered the light and the heavy-weight cattle. The treaty with Mexico covered the medium-weight cattle; and the immediate effect, if the treaty is denounced, is to take away the tariff concession that arises to Canada, out of the agreement between Mexico and the United

States, on medium-weight cattle. Naturally the item is down for discussion at Torquay, and I have every reason to believe that medium-weight cattle will be brought under the general agreement on tariffs and trade.

Can the minister say something on the news item-I think I saw it in the New York Times of Sunday-to the effect that the hoped-for removal of administrative restrictions in the American tariff is not likely or that the bill before congress is not likely to be passed this year? Can the minister comment on that matter? I understand that in some ways administrative restrictions are more important than the actual tariffs.

The bill in question is still
before a committee of the United States congress. I would not want to take responsibility for saying it will not be passed, and I am sure my hon. friend would not. That is a matter for the United States congress, I think.

Minister of Trade and Commerce is giving passes. Perhaps that is the reason for all the deficit on the Trans-Canada Air Lines.

The minister should give us a little statement regarding this international trade fair. I have now attended, I think, three of these fairs in Toronto and the third seemed to be a wonderful fair. It would appear from this item that it is going to be continued for another year. The 1950 Canadian international trade fair ended on June 9. The merchandise of 2,247 manufacturers and producers from 33 countries, including Canada, was shown during the previous two weeks. It will be appreciated that as yet it is too early to get final costs and revenues, but from present figures available it would appear that the costs are $835,000 and the revenue $442,000, an estimated net cost of $393,000.
The number of business visitors who were registered as being in attendance is 35,364. While the majority of these were from Canada, there were business representatives registered at the fair from many countries. While no effort is made by the Canadian government exhibition commission to secure exact figures from the individual exhibitors as to the business conducted at the fair, judging from the comments volunteered by a number of the exhibitors there is no doubt this fair has been the most successful of the three held to date.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
The fair has several purposes. It enables Canadian buyers to view the work of many countries and compare the products of one country with another. The limiting factor on the number of buyers who attended the fair was the hotel accommodation in Toronto and vicinity. The fair permits Canadian manufacturers to compare their products with those of other countries and also to compare Canadian prices with those of other lands. It brings many visitors to Canada who are potential customers for Canadian products. I found the Canadian exhibitors just as enthusiastic about the results obtained from the fair as were the other exhibitors, particularly those from the United Kingdom.

I am glad to hear the minister make that statement. I attended the fair and I think it is a wonderful institution. If the house is sitting when the next fair is on I think it should close for two or three days to give all hon. members an opportunity to attend. One could see only a portion of the exhibits in a day but it gave a good impression of what industry was doing in other countries. It was a marvellous sight to see all these countries showing their wares and offering them for sale, and incidentally making a number of sales.

438.	Salaries and other expenses, $26,450.

I should like to say a few words about this item. It involves a little matter of nearly $600 million belonging to the wheat growers of the prairie provinces. It has given me and the wheat growers of the west

quite a lot of concern since the British wheat agreement was made some three or four years ago. Earlier this month we were able to get a statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that the British government does not intend to make good anything in connection with the "have regard to" clause in the British wheat agreement. Tonight I hope he will tell us what the government intends to do to make up the western farmers' losses, and I hope he will not tell us that the government feels that the farmers have not any money coming to them, because at least some members of the government are not of that opinion.
Under the contract we supplied Great Britain with wheat in 1946-47 at $1.55 a bushel, and the average price of class II wheat, which can be called by any name you wish but I call it class II wheat because we are dealing with wheat sold by the Canadian wheat board and for which they received payment, was $2.43 a bushel. That involved an average loss of 88 cents a bushel on the wheat sold to Great Britain. In the 194-7-48 crop year we supplied wheat to Great Britain at $1.55 a bushel, and the Canadian wheat board was able to sell class II wheat to its different customers at $2.88 a bushel, or a loss to the Canadian wheat grower of $1.33 a bushel. In the third year of the contract, the 1948-49 crop year, Great Britain paid us $2 per bushel while the average price for class II wheat was $2.23 per bushel, meaning a loss of 23 cents a bushel, or more than $400 million for the three crop years.
During the same period we supplied millers with wheat so that the people of Canada could eat cheap bread, at a cost to the farmers of approximately $124 million. Those two sums total $524 million up to the present time, and we expect that there will be further losses on the present crop year. What they are I am not prepared to state. Since I do not want to be contradicted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce or anybody else I have used approximate figures, because actual figures are not very easy to obtain. We may be told that the Canadian wheat growers are not entitled to any compensation. To prove my case I want to quote from page 1971 of Hansard for March 24, 1949. The house was dealing at that time with the Agricultural Products Act. Near the bottom of the second column we find that the Minister of Agriculture had this to say:
Along with that consideration I couple the fact that it is due to the farmers of this country that we have legislation such as this on our statute books throughout the transitional period in order that the house may see to it that the whole population of
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Canada pays back some of what my hon. friends over on the other side of the house have been talking about ever since this debate began.
Ever since this house held its first sitting in this session, member after member has been getting up and saying: Why should the farmer carry the whole load? What I am saying to this house tonight is that the government does not believe that the farmer should carry the whole load.
I ask the committee to take particular note of that statement made by the Minister of Agriculture. He went on to say:
We have arrived at the time when, unless we are going to make an effort to have Canada carry part of the load, we must throw our farmers on other markets and put them in the position of having to take a lower price than they can get under these contracts, and a lower price than they ought to be able to get in Canada, because of what they have done over the past seven or eight years. When we put that emergency alongside of the other emergency, then I say that there is every reason in the world for passing this piece of legislation which has in it only one section of importance, which says that this kind of legislation should be continued for another year. During that year we hope we may be able to do at least some of the things Canada ought to do in order to express appreciation of all that the farmers did throughout the war, and since.
The Minister of Agriculture has made several statements about these losses. I should like to refer to what he had to say on December 10, 1949, when discussing his estimates. He was referring at the time to a speech he made to the London chamber of commerce in December, 1948. At page 3079 of Hansard he had this to say:
The trend of the article is to call attention to the fact, not in this country but over in Great Britain, that it is a pretty difficult task for twelve million people to undertake to feed, half feed or twenty-five per cent feed, fifty million people in Great Britain. If that is what is being suggested, then I am quite prepared to say that if it is going to be done it cannot be done by the farmers alone.
For that reason I say the Minister of Agriculture, even if he has no support in the cabinet, is willing to admit and has admitted that the farmers of Canada should not carry this whole load by themselves. I have said that it is not the business of the farmers to demand that Britain make good any further losses. That should be a matter between the British government and the Canadian government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and his officials were over there earlier this month. They were told by Sir Stafford Cripps and his officials that Britain had fulfilled its share of the contract, and on behalf of Canada the minister stated that they agreed with that pronouncement. So I feel the remainder of the responsibility lies directly upon the dominion government.
Time after time we on this side of the house have asked the government to give us some statement in connection with those losses. Tonight I hope the minister will tell
4164	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce us what the government intend to do about that matter. The farmers of the west feel that they did a fairly good job during the war. They worked long hours; they worked hard, and then had their products taken over by the government and in some instances sold' at give-away prices. Now they demand some compensation for what was done in the past. Many of us felt that we would have a guaranteed market at guaranteed prices for at least seven or eight years to offset the losses accepted under those wheat agreements and in connection with the sale of other products, but at present we find practically no protection, no guaranteed markets and no guaranteed prices. Our wheat is being sold under the international wheat agreement, and in that I find very little protection for our farmers. So I believe the time is now at hand, since the period ends on July 31, for the government to come through with what the farmers really believed they intended to do; that is, make up the losses suffered under the contracts with Great Britain and through the sale of our wheat at prices which were kept low in order that we might maintain price control and a low cost of living in Canada during the war and for some years after.

I agree with the sentiments that have been expressed by the hon. member for Battle River. Because of government policy over the past number of years the farmers have made a real sacrifice for the benefit of the Canadian consumer, and also for the benefit of our best export customer, Great Britain. I agree with the hon. member when he says the government has some obligation to take care of at least part of the loss that has been incurred, and a continuing obligation over the years ahead to give the farmers stability. I know the Saskatchewan farmers' union and the Alberta farmers' union had a conference with the minister last week, during which they presented a brief which dealt with two main points. The first was that the government had an obligation to make up some of the losses sustained by farmers who have sold their wheat since 1945, and also a continuing obligation to guarantee reasonable prices in the future. I should like to ask the minister if the government has reached a decision as to what additional payment might be expected over and above whatever amount is left in the wheat pool fund. Did the minister hear my question?
Yes, I heard it.
And if a decision has not been reached I should like to know if the matter is still under consideration and whether a decision will be reached soon.
My hon. friend is talking about-

I should like to make a short comment before the minister replies. I agree with some of the remarks of the hon. member for Battle River and the hon. member for Assiniboia; but they both paint a lurid picture in which they make out that the farmer of western Canada is destitute. I cannot agree with that.
Mr. Chairman, that is something the hon. member has drawn from his imagination.

Kindly let me finish. I allowed you to go on; now let me talk. I have listened to you fellows for the last four months. You are like a bunch of jacks-in-the-box; whenever anyone tries to say anything you jump to your feet. Now let me say a word. I do not want anyone to get the idea that I have not the interests of the western farmer at heart just as much as any one of you.
Better express it, then.

If you will be quiet long enough I shall do so. Do not forget the position of the western farmer in 1939. At that time the average farmer had a mortgage on his farm; he was heavily in debt; he had no car, and no machinery. Look at his position ten years later.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who was in power then?

Never mind; certainly it was not the C.C.F. Ten years later we find the western farmer in a pretty solid position. He has paid off his mortgage; he has a reasonable quantity of good machinery and a car too in which to take the odd little holiday. The hon. member for Assiniboia spoke of the Saskatchewan farmers' union pleading with the government-
Not pleading.
I get a great kick out of these fellows over here, Mr. Chairman. I sit and suffer; and I say "suffer" advisedly-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You mean you sit and slumber.

-and listen to them for six months, but they have not the courtesy to let someone else speak without interruption. I cannot say what I have in mind at the moment or I will be called to order, but I really feel sorry for their intelligence.
That will hold them.
Nothing will hold them; they do not know any better.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If we did not interrupt, you would have nothing to say.

There is the hon. gentleman who has spoken about eight hundred times, who bobs up like a jumping jack. Never in my life have I heard anyone who knew so much about so little and had so much to say about it. There is nothing mentioned in this house on which he is not an expert. The hon. member for Assiniboia spoke of the period from 1940 to 1945. I quite appreciate that farm prices were not too high, but we must not forget that all prices in Canada were fixed, and relatively speaking during the war years the farmers were reasonably well treated.
I said in 1945.
You mentioned the money that was owed up to 1945.
I said from 1945 on.

I quite agree that the price was not high, but neither were the wages of the average industrial worker. In 1945 and 1946 the question of a fair price for wheat was under discussion, and it will be recalled that the wheat pools and farm organizations throughout Canada were quite happy and quite ready to agree on a five-year price of $1.55 per bushel. I believe the minister will back me up in that. All right; we have gone on these last few years, and at the present time the price to the farmer is fixed at $1.75 a bushel for all the wheat he will have delivered during the five crop years ending July 31. I should like to suggest to the minister that, in view of the fact that our freight rates in western Canada are rising because labour wants more money, when the government starts discussing the winding up of this wheat board operation they will consider giving the farmer an additional fifteen cents per bushel. Just for my information, how much is it?
Knowing as much as you let on you know, you ought to know that without my telling you.
You just don't know.
You know, when I look at the hon. gentlemen over there who let on they know so many things, I feel sorry for them.
What are you talking about?
You would not know; you have not reached that state of maturity.

I just asked one simple question. Give me an answer to it.

At the moment I am not in a position to discuss it. I am sure my hon. friend knows less about the situation than I do, and I can assure him he is in no position to discuss it.

With respect to item 439, the matter to which I wish to refer has to do with the inspection department of the grain board under the Canada Grain Act. I have had a number of complaints recently of the quality of western feed grain being shipped to eastern Canada. I know the standards that are required for the various grades when we sell, for instance 3 C.W. oats and No. 1 feed oats and 3 C.W. barley or No. 3 barley. If the report's that are received from the purchasers in eastern Canada are correct, there must be mixing of those grades somewhere between the time they leave the country elevator in western Canada and the time they reach the farmer in eastern Canada. It is my understanding that under the Canada Grain Act there are certain standards for various grades of grain, as regards both in-turn standards and out-turn standards being shipped from Port Arthur and Fort William. I would ask the minister if the standards for the grades of, let us say, 3 C.W. oats as they are sold on the farm are the same standards as are used for that same grade as sold to eastern buyers.
I understand that the standards are practically the same and that, if mixing takes place, it is most likely that rt takes place after the grain has been bought by the eastern dealers, and that it is mixed before it is

sold to the farmer. I think we should have some assurance from the minister with respect to these grades.
Just recently, for instance, a man came to me and said that a shipment of Argentine oats that had been brought into Canada just recently was of a better quality than a similar grade of Canadian oats. If our standards are maintained, or if the grades are maintained on those oats that are sold in western Canada until they reach eastern Canada, I know that our grades will compare favourably with the standards of oats or any other feed grain grown in any other part of the world. If there is mixing taking place, I think we should be able to find out under this item where it is taking place, and I think it should be stopped.

I might say incidentally that the hon. member's friend who told him the quality of Argentine oats was better than that of Canadian oats perhaps did not have the facts to back up that statement, because no Argentine oats have been delivered in this country as yet. That shipment is not due until July 15. So my hon. friend can tell him that perhaps he does not know what he is talking about.
He had samples.

I can say, however, that
Argentine oats do not rank with Canadian feed oats in quality. They are well below that grade. However, the standards of feed grain are exactly the same in western Canada as they are in eastern Canada. As it passes through the board facilities, the grain is inspected at the lakehead, using exactly the same standards that apply as when the grain is bought in the country. If the grain is shipped to a board elevator in the east-that is the board of grain commissioners' public elevator-the standard of shipment out of that elevator is exactly the same as the standards in western Canada. But my hon. friend will appreciate the fact that the board of grain commissioners has no control of grain once it passes into distribution in the province of Ontario. Its handling is then a matter for provincial legislation. We have not the complementary provincial legislation in Ontario that we have in the three western provinces. Therefore anything could happen to the grain from the time that it passes out of the board's facilities into the system of distribution.

That is exactly the answer I
expected the minister to make, and I think that is correct. If there is mixing taking place with respect to this grain, I think that it takes place after it reaches the province of Ontario here and after it goes out of the hands of the board of grain commissioners and out of the hands of the wheat board. It is up to
Supply-Trade and Commerce the eastern provinces themselves to set standards for their feed grain which will protect their own farmers.

Will the
minister say something about the international wheat council which we pay $25,000 to belong to? Just what have been its duties in the past and what can we expect from it in the future?

The international wheat council is the regulatory body that administers the international wheat agreement. The wheat agreement came into effect only on July 31 last. The council administers all international transactions. All transactions under the agreement are registered by the council. The council notifies participating countries when they have taken up their full quota. If any exporting country wishes to put grain, as it has a right to do, under the agreement, the allocation of that grain is made by the central council. It is an important administrative body in the world grain trade and one in which Canada is glad to claim membership.

Does our
British agreement go through it?

No. That agreement is registered under it, but the agreement with Britain was a bilateral one that carried over from the days before the international agreement. After July 31, all our transactions will be made through the council instead of by bilateral agreement.

Item agreed to.
Canada Grain Act-

The minister will recall that one May 31 I was asking some questions with regard to an extension of the Canada Grain Act to apply in southwestern Ontario. The growers and I appreciate what the minister had to say at that time with a view to extending it at the next revision of the Canada Grain Act. Since that time I have found that certain things have already been done in southwestern Ontario under the Canada Grain Act, and it would appear that it would apply in that area without any amendments or changes to the act. I am just going to draw this to the minister's attention. I am referring to the statement of the minister in answer to a question of mine on May 31, as reported at page 3035 of Hansard:

It includes white beans, so-called.
Soybeans are graded by the province of Ontario, assisted by the Department of Agriculture of the federal government. It is questionable whether the

Supply-Trade and Commerce board of grain commissioners would have the constitutional authority to grade grains which are grown and consumed in the one province. The board of grain commissioners handles grain that moves in interprovincial traffic or for export.
He doubted whether it would apply in domestic trade. Then on page 6 of the annual report of the board for the year 1938, the following statement appears:
Inspection Services in Western Ontario
In response to requests from the corn growers of western Ontario on September 15, the board opened an office in Chatham and inaugurated voluntary inspection service in this region for the purpose of grading com and other grain grown.
Then on page 8 of the annual report of the board of grain commissioners for the year 1942, we find this statement:
Grading of Soybeans and Flax
Under order in council P.C. 2799 dated April 10, 1942, the Canadian wheat board was authorized to purchase soybeans, and requested the board to make provision for the grading thereof.
After discussions with representatives of the producers and handlers, the board prepared specifications for the different grades of soybeans and these were authorized by order in council P.C. 6125, dated July 16, 1942.
To give you some idea of what is being handled through the Chatham office, the eastern grain division reported that at Montreal there were 1,590 cars inspected; at Toronto, 2,033 cars inspected; while at Chatham there were 8,337 cars inspected. That will give some idea of the volume of business there. I hope that he will look into the desires of the growers in southwestern Ontario, and make the Canada Grain Act applicable to that area. Will the minister give us an answer to that at least?

I am aware that the board of grain commissioners inspect eastern grain, but I understand such inspection is voluntary. That is, any shipper can have his grain graded by the board of grain commissioners if he wishes, or not, if he does not wish to.
I understood the remarks of my hon. friend were applied to compulsory grading of eastern grain. As I understand the situation, it is not compulsory; it is voluntary. It is a service the board of grain commissioners offer if anyone wishes to take advantage of it. Is that correct?
It would not be too difficult to make it operative in western Ontario. They would not have to amend the grain act to do that.
We would have to get the permission of the province of Ontario. I doubt whether we have the constitutional jurisdiction to impose compulsory inspection in Ontario.
You work on that, and I will also.
Yes, quite.
Can the minister give a brief definition of the duties of the board of grain commissioners?

This is the definition in my book: For necessary services provided under the provisions of the Canada Grain Act in connection with the supervision and handling of grain from delivery at country elevators to delivery to vessels for export, including the licensing and bonding of elevators and grain dealers; sampling, inspection and grading of grain; setting of standards or grades of grain; weighing the grain at terminal elevators; registration of warehouse receipts; collecting and collating grain statistics; maintenance of grain research laboratory and collection of fees for services rendered.
I was wondering what effect the creation and operation of the wheat board would have upon the duties of that board. I mean whether it would lessen their work or make it greater.
I doubt whether it has any effect one way or the other. The wheat board is a marketing organization; whereas the board of grain commissioners is a licensing organization.
How many assistant commissioners are there, and where are they situated?
There are three commissioners, as my hon. friend knows, stationed in Winnipeg, and there are assistant commissioners at Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon and Fort William.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
When this item was up for discussion on December 10 of last year I had a few words with the minister concerning the question of the five-day week for employees working under the board of grain commissioners in the inspection offices associated with the railway yards in Winnipeg. The minister may recall that 1 pointed out to him at that time that these people are civil servants, and that they were concerned as to why, in view of the general five-day week in the civil service during the summer, they were not given a five-day week last summer. I took it up with the minister in the middle of December although that was not an opportune time to talk about conditions in the summertime. He did point out to me then, however, that the matter was under consideration. Obviously there were certain difficulties, but I gathered from what he said -and I read it again today to check on it-

that it was a point that should be looked into and perhaps something could be done about it one way or the other. Can the minister say whether arrangements have been made for the five-day week for these inspection employees this summer?

No arrangements have been made. The trouble is that the board of grain commissioners is a servicing institution, and it must provide service whenever the services are 'required. It is something like the post office in that respect. My hon. friend knows that the post office does not have a five-day week either because it is required to give service on six days. No plan has been worked out-in fact I think it would be unreasonable for the employees to expect that they will have a five-day week in the busy season of their operation. Perhaps if they had asked for the five-day week in April or May, or particularly in March or April, it would be quite easy to work out. But the summer season is the busy season in the grain business. speechtext: That is substantially what the minister said when I raised this question on December 10 last, except that at that time having said that he thought it was difficult to work out a five-day week in the summertime he said that something might be done by way of time oft at another time of the year in lieu of the five-day week in the summertime. Can the minister say whether or not the decision of the board of grain commissioners to reduce or to degrade Red Bobs wheat down to No. 3 was the result of criticism by the foreign customers?

Yes. Many complaints were received from abroad that the quality of wheat being shipped as No. 1 northern from the west coast was not up to the quality of the same grade being shipped from the east coast. To what extent are these government elevators being used for the purpose for which they were created? That is to say, what is their percentage of efficiency? I do not know whether that is the correct term. What percentage of their capacity is being used? I want to draw to the attention of the minister-I have done it before-the fact that the government elevator at Saskatoon is a very fine building and has a capacity of 5J million bushels. In the last number of years since I have been a member of this house there has not been enough grain put through it to keep the machinery from rusting. I should like to know for example how much money the operation of that elevator has been costing the taxpayers of this country, and whether there is any means by which it can be used more. Now that there is a change in the market situation -it is an ill wind that blows no one good- I hope that in the future that elevator may be used more. Perhaps the minister would comment on these various questions.

I can assure my hon. friend that the elevator is being used exactly for the purpose for which it was built. I know the purpose for which it was built, because I was associated with the board of grain commissioners when it was built. It was built as emergency storage and it is being used for that purpose. When the grain backs up so that it cannot be handled through the normal export channels-I mean the normal channels that move grain from the farm to market-* then interior storages are filled, and interior terminals are very handy for that purpose. That is the purpose for which they were built, and that is the purpose for which they are being used. But my hon. friend would not expect me to subordinate the marketing of grain to the use of any storage in elevators. The grain must move to market expeditiously; it must be put in position so that it can be sold without any side interests being concerned, and that is being done. I think perhaps the elevators will be used this year because there seems to be a promise of an exceptionally large crop. If that large crop does develop, as I believe it will, these interior storage terminal elevators will be used for the purposes for which they were built, emergency storage.
Item agreed to.

Canada Grain Act-
442.	Canadian government elevators, including equipment (revote $144,628), $741,085.

Where are these elevators located and do they appear anywhere as a government asset? I have not been able to find them in the statement given us by the Minister of Finance, although I have not read it through as carefully as I might have. Will the minister give us some information as to their capital value and as to just what this item covers?

It covers the handling of grain at elevators at Calgary, Edmonton, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Lethbridge. The board also administers an elevator at Port Arthur which is under lease at this time to a grain company. Under the peculiar system used by the government in these matters, the receipts from these elevators go into a different account and do not appear in these estimates.
Why don't you change that?
It would reduce the size of the estimates considerably if we did, but that does not come within my jurisdiction.
Were they built by the government?
Yes.

Will the
minister tell us how much revenue there actually was under this quaint system of accounting?

Since these elevators have been built they have returned a profit which has completely amortized their cost. I happen to know that although that fact does not appear in this item. The total grain handled last year amounted to 3,031,809 bushels, of which 2,227,703 bushels were handled at the Calgary elevator. The net result of the operations for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1949, was a deficit of $222,565.11, as compared with a deficit of $131,282.90 in the previous fiscal year. When there is no emergency the handlings in these elevators are quite small, but once we have a surplus crop, the elevators earn money very rapidly. Over the years they have proved a profitable investment.

I want to commend the minister for the reply he made to the hon. member for Saskatoon. I live close to that elevator the hon. member spoke of and I know that the western farmer is pleased that that elevator is not full all the time. That indicates that our wheat is moving.

Item agreed to.
Terminable services-
445.	To provide for production and transportation subsidies on steel and iron under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $2,000,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

This is part of the transition of the wartime steel structure into peacetime and it is hoped that this will be the last time this item will appear as we expect to liquidate the subsidy situation by March 31 of next year. Through these subsidies we have been able to integrate the steel capacity of Canada and use it to the maximum. We did it first to overcome a difficult supply problem and we are doing it now in order to have the full use of these facilities, at least until the end of this year.
The assistance policy has had a pronounced effect on prices with the result that Canadian prices are lower than Pittsburgh prices, something unknown in pre-war years. Low prices for steel have played an important part in stimulating industry, both for internal distribution and export. At the present time we pay for the movement of semi-finished steel from Sydney to Hamilton and from Sault Ste. Marie to Hamilton, the purpose being to make sure that that semi-finished steel is produced to full Canadian capacity in the first place, and finished in Canada, in the second, place, in order to make full use of all the finishing capacity in the country.

Has the government any plans in mind for increasing steel production in Canada and building up a balanced and complete iron and steel industry? I ask that because of two developments that have

occurred, the one at Steep Rock, Ontario, where it is expected within a few years they will be producing 7 million tons of iron ore a year, and the other the development in northern Quebec and Labrador. From what appears in the press it would appear that big changes are about to take place in the iron and steel industry of this continent. I have here a dispatch which appeared in the Financial Times of June 23 which reads:
American Steel Industry to be Revolutionized by New Iron Ore Sources
Huge deposits being opened up In Ungava-Labrador and in Venezuela will mean move of steel plants to Atlantic seaboard: speeding up in New Quebec-Labrador project important.
I am not in position to state whether or not that report is accurate, but it would appear that there are tremendous possibilities for Canada. I wish the minister would state whether there is as yet any government policy for the increase of our iron and steel production. For example, will it be possible to use this Canadian iron ore to increase the production of steel on Cape Breton island, and would it be possible to erect steel plants along the St. Lawrence river. What does the minister think are the possibilities brought about by this immense body of ore in northern Quebec and Labrador as well as the development at Steep Rock? To a layman it would appear that Canada is on the threshold of a tremendous development largely because of these resources and I would like the minister to give us some information as to just what the future may hold for Canada in this regard.

The Canadian steel industry
has more than doubled in the last ten years and it continues to expand. New blast furnace capacity is at present being built in Hamilton and a new finishing mill is being installed at Sault Ste. Marie. The industry never stops expanding. It attempts to take care of Canadian requirements, and I am sure that it will succeed in doing so. As I say, great strides have been made in the last several years. The policy of the government has been to make that development possible. We helped the industry by subsidy over a difficult period, and the reason that we are stopping the subsidy at the end of this year is that the transition is being made, plants are getting into balance, and we think government-assisted interchange of primary steel between plants will no longer be needed for this year. We have been net importers of iron ore through the years. We are coming into the position of a net exporter, for which I am very happy, and the larger the exports are after the needs of Canadian industry have been supplied the happier I shall be.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

Would the minister care to
comment upon the statement he made last fall in which he indicated that the discoveries of large iron ore deposits in Quebec and Labrador in all probability would mean that the St. Lawrence deep waterway project was going to be started very soon. I have not his exact words, but I know that was the effect of the statement he made. Will he indicate to the committee whether, in his opinion, it is likely to have that development?

My hon. friend knows the difficulty about starting the St. Lawrence development. He knows that we signed a treaty to do our part many years ago, and we are waiting for the United States to sign a treaty. As soon as it is signed the work will commence. I think what I suggested in my earlier discussion was that the iron ore in Labrador will create large tonnage traffic in the opposite direction from the present flow of traffic in the St. Lawrence canals, and that balanced traffic should be an inducement to assist in the financing of the waterway.

The iron ore has to be
smelted in the upper lakes region.
Have you made any represensations to the United States government?

I have indeed, and I have the assurance of several members of their cabinet that it is the wish of the administration that this legislation be enacted. I feel sure an effort will be made to obtain the legislation while the present administration is in power.
Is there anything in the suggestion in the Financial Times that the United States steel industry is likely to move to the Atlantic coast?

I would not believe it on the
strength of the say-so of the Financial Times.

Is there a possibility of that
happening? Is that the trend, not only because of Canadian iron ore but also because of the Venezuela ore?

I have in mind that it costs at least three times as much to build a steel plant today as it did in pre-war days. I doubt very much if even a country as wealthy as the United States could do away with the steel plant in Pittsburgh and build a new steel plant on the Atlantic coast, with no greater inducement than a lower freight rate on its iron ore.
The decrease of $5,750,000 in that one item is quite a sizeable amount. What I should like to find out is whether all of the $7,750,000 was spent last year?

Yes, practically all.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
How was it allocated between the three operating companies, Algoma, Dosco and Stelco?

It was not allocated to companies. It was paid out largely as a freight subvention. If steel moving to Hamilton was bought f.o.b. Sydney the government paid the transportation, and it was sold at the Sydney price f.o.b. Hamilton. It is like the coal subvention which is paid to the railways. I am not sure that the steel subvention was paid directly to the railway, but that was the effect of it. It was the rail rate that was subsidized rather than any particular company. Last year there were certain scrap subsidies. Companies that had to go abroad for scrap, or had to go into uneconomical areas, were subsidized for their scrap movements. In other words, if prairie scrap had to be moved to Hamilton or Sault Ste. Marie, or foreign scrap had to be moved into Sydney, it was subsidized, but the scrap subsidies were suspended at the end of the last fiscal year.
I had a return on the subsidy that Dosco received, and it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,500,000. None of this money was used for plant expansion at all?
No.
And you think $2 million will be adequate to subsidize the movement of steel?
Yes, we think so.

I am interested in this item because I am interested in steel, which is one of the basic industries of Nova Scotia, With regard to what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra had to say about the possibilities of steel in the future on the Atlantic seaboard. I am not very much impressed with the forecast that the iron ore deposits in Newfoundland are going to benefit Canada to any great extent. I made up my mind on that point in 1947 when the present Postmaster General was piloting a bill through the house to grant rights to certain exploration companies not only to explore deposits in Quebec and Labrador but also to develop railroads, bus lines, hotel facilities and so on over the period of the next ten years. I made up my mind then that, so far as Canada was concerned, she was selling her future rights to the ore in those areas.
There were a couple of members who tried to tell the house at that time as best we could that all we were doing was granting a franchise to Canadian companies fronting for United States capital. The tie-up with United States companies such as M. A. Hanna, National Steel and others was quite apparent.

If you will go deep enough I think you will find that the stock in Canadian steel companies is largely held in the United States. If we are going to tie the two countries together in that way it is all right, but I opposed that kind of thing at that time as a Canadian who wanted to see Canadian resources developed for Canadians. I think you are three years too late in hoping that the great ore deposits of Labrador and Ungava will mean very much to us.
I believe that there will be a swing of some of the United States companies to the Atlantic seaboard. I know that at least one company is establishing a large fabricating plant in the eastern states. Unless there are drastic changes in our thinking on that matter, I think we are too late so far as iron ore and the future of steel production in Canada is concerned. We have already sold our rights for a period of ten years at least. I was wondering why there should be such a sharp drop in this item because if a subsidy of $1,500,000 to Dosco was necessary last year to transport its raw steel to central Canada the other steel companies are not going to get very much out of the $2 million. About all that Dosco is doing is producing raw material and shipping it to Quebec and Ontario for processing to be sent somewhere else. I know that a subsidy is necessary to move steel from eastern to central Canada, and I was wondering if the cut was not a little too drastic.
My hon. friend says if the material is exported no benefit to Canada ensues. Aluminum is a raw material produced in Canada, of which 95 per cent or possibly 97 per cent is exported.
That is manufactured, is it not?
Well, it is smelted, just as copper is smelted.
Bauxite is the raw material.

And that is imported into the country. The only thing the aluminum company uses in this country is water power; everything else is imported. It is said that we export our power in the form of aluminum; but that industry supports some twenty-five thousand employees, and we receive about $20 million a year in taxes. There we have an industry that has spent a few hundred million dollars in the Saguenay district and is prepared to do the same thing on the west coast. So 1 do not think there is any great loss to the country because of the fact that 97 per cent of the aluminum coming from that plant is exported.
In the same way you might say the Nor-anda copper mine is a perfect example of

the loss of Canadian resources. I suppose 70 per cent of the copper coming out of that mine goes out of the country. Nevertheless it is the centre of a great industrial population, and I cannot see that because the primary copper is largely exported from the country my hon. friend should say that an industry of this kind is of no benefit to Canada. The development of the Labrador iron ore deposits will create a source of that product in Canada, which will be available to Canadians if it is required. After all, Canada owns that resource, whatever the source of the money going into its development. As long as it is situated in Canada that resource belongs to this country and is subject to our law, whether emergency or ordinary legislation. I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that about $250 million of somebody's money has to be invested in that operation before a hundred tons of ore are delivered at seaboard. In other words $250 million has to be invested before there is any return whatever from the property. Does my hon. friend suggest that an investment of that amount in an undeveloped area of Canada is not good for the Canadian economy? If he does, I must say I cannot agree.

I did not say this industry was of no benefit. At the same time, if we are just planning to continue to be hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States, we are not thinking very far ahead. I am not satisfied with that. The aluminum industry, as a straight exporter of raw materials, may bring in $80 million or $180 million a year, but I think we should at least make a start in building an industry that will process our own raw materials in our own country. I believe we should regard it as a trust to develop this country to the best of our ability, thinking in terms of the coming generation.
I am not satisfied with the automobile industry. We have steel, copper and all the materials that go into the manufacture of an automobile. We are exporting these materials to the United States, and in Canada we have plants which are assembling automobiles. If I go to Windsor or Oshawa to buy a car, I pay from 35 to 50 per cent more than it costs in the United States. What is wrong with our making a start, somewhere in this country, on building up a Canadian automobile industry, and knocking off that tariff which is put on at the border to protect those who are exporting raw materials from this country? I think that is wrong. While we may be getting something out of the materials we are sending out of the country, we are not getting as much as we would if we had an industry that would process our own raw materials.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
I am thinking in terms of that steel plant at Sydney, which produces a third or a fifth of Canada's raw steel. As a nation we are not losing anything on that operation because there are fabricating plants in central Canada; but that material is exported from the maritimes and processed in this part of the country, and then if we want to use some of the finished product down there we have that long freight haul to contend with, which adds to the cost. I want to see a tinplate industry built around that plant at Sydney. I believe the sheet mill that was operating during the war should have been continued, because we are importing ninety per cent of our steel plate from the United States, and there are all kinds of possibilities for small investments in the maritimes to build an industry around that mill.
Fertilizer is another matter. I know the minister remembers that during the war, through the department of reconstruction and supply, he spent quite a bit of money in research at that plant in connection with fertilizer. The research has been done, and I believe it should be possible to establish a fertilizer plant where we had one previously. That plant was moved out. Instead of a plant there, we are subsidizing the freight cost on fertilizer moving to the maritimes, and then when the farmer gets it he must pay an exorbitant price.
I am not being critical of the minister; perhaps during the period through which we have gone it was necessary to do things that way; but no one can convince me that we did right by handing over the leases for the Ungava and Labrador resources, after we had done the exploration work for ten years. It seems to me $250 million would have been a small investment to protect the future of this country in that area. I do not believe it could not have been obtained in this country. I believe that with the proper encouragement and sales talk by dominion and provincial authorities, that money could have been found as risk capital. In the final analysis, it seems to me that whole project could have been financed through the Bank of Canada. During the war when the minister of munitions and supply, who is now the Minister of Trade and Commerce, wanted a munitions plant put up, or a gun factory, he did not think about the cost. He just decided it had to be done; he asked if we had the material and the people to operate it, then supplied the credit to put up the plant and get it going. He did an excellent job, and I believe he could have done the same thing in connection with this Ungava development. I am sure $250 million could have been found in this country, but we have sold the birthright of

Supply-Trade and Commerce future Canadians in that area and one of our basic industries will be undeveloped, because I am convinced that the future of steel is on the Atlantic seaboard; and we have lost control of it.

My hon. friend suggests that Canada does nothing to develop a steel industry here, that we are simply hewers of wood and drawers of water for the United States. I suggest that Canada built her steel industry and had other people as hewers of wood and drawers of water. There was no iron ore in Nova Scotia when the Dominion Steel plant was built. You had to go to Newfoundland, a foreign country, for your ore. There was no iron ore on the Canadian side of the great lakes when the great steel industry at Hamilton and Sault Ste. Marie was developed. All that ore was obtained from the other side of the great lakes. In other words the United States were the hewers of wood and drawers of water for Canada, as far as iron ore was concerned, until two or three years ago. On balance it is probably supplying us with more iron ore today than we are giving it. I have never heard public men in the United States complain of being hewers of wood and drawers of water for Canadians. They were very glad to sell us their surplus iron ore, just as I think we are very glad to sell them our surplus. Certainly we will have a steel industry that will be based on the requirements of this country, and our steel men will be delighted to put in the capacity to the full extent they are able to sell the product. They always have been, and they will continue to be. If we can develop a greater capacity for the iron ore, we will be delighted to sell it abroad just as we sell our wheat, and a good many other raw materials. We are not hewers of wood and drawers of water for Europe just because we sell our surplus wheat in Europe. I think that applies to any of our raw materials, whether it be iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, or anything we produce in quantities above what we are able to consume in this country.
My hon. friend speaks of the automobile manufacturers being assembly plants. I would suggest to him that approximately 80 per cent of the automobiles made by the three principal companies in Canada are Canadian products. In the vicinity of those automobile plants, he will find a great many subsidiary plants that are making parts for these automobiles. If they are assembly plants, then they are assembling materials that are 80 per cent Canadian finished.

Would it not be possible for Canada, because of these huge deposits of iron ore, to develop a steel industry which could
IMr. Gillis.l
export steel? Could we not produce steel which would form a foundation upon which we could provide jobs for many millions more people than we have at the present time? Could we not only meet our own requirements, but also export steel and bring more people here because of this resource?
I do not know where we would find an export market for any great volume. Every country tries to be self-sufficient in steel. We could not export to Great Britain, or to the continent.
What about Asia?
What part of Asia would my friend suggest, and what would they use for money?
Over the long run?
Over the long run we may try to do it, but I think today if we look after our Canadian requirements for steel we are taking care of the market that is open to us.

If the St. Lawrence waterway is built, will that mean there will be new steel plants on the Canadian side of the great lakes, lake Ontario or lake Erie, or would practically all that iron be used on the United States side at the present steel ports? Will it mean any development of a steel industry in Canada, or will it merely mean the sale of the raw iron to the United States, replacing the iron ore from the Mesabi range?

Mr. Chairman, a prudent manufacturer makes what he thinks he can sell. He does not ordinarily worry about the raw materials, so long as he can get them at reasonable prices. That is the easy part, but the difficult part is to sell the product he undertakes to manufacture. I can tell my hon. friend that if there is any Canadian entrepreneur who thinks he can sell more steel than he is selling at present, the chances are that he will make it because that is where his profit comes from. My hon. friend is just as competent as I am to decide how much more steel a manufacturer is capable of making. I hope he is not suggesting that we should process in Canada every ounce of iron ore produced in Canada?
No one is suggesting that.
That is the result of your "Canada first" argument.

If we are going to get into this "Canada first" argument, it will be a real one. I am not arguing that all of Canada's iron ore should be turned into steel in Canada. I quite agree that the surplus must be sold. But here we have these tremendous discoveries, and I am hoping that they can be the cause of a tremendous development in

Canada, and the magnet which will attract a great many people to our shores. What worries me is whether that is the objective of the government or whether the only objective is to sell iron ore to the United States?
The government shares your hope.
I am glad that they do. They are waking up at last, perhaps.

I know the people of Nova Scotia appreciate the subsidies that have been paid out in recent years to assist m the movement of coal and iron from Nova Scotia. I am in agreement with my fellow member from Nova Scotia, the member for Cape Breton South, that we should encourage the processing of these raw materials in Canada. That is one of the main complaints of the people of Nova Scotia, and it applies to what has been done under this subsidy. Our steel and iron produced in Nova Scotia are largely shipped in crude form to places in central Canada. We should have the refining plants near the source of production in Nova Scotia, so that we would derive greater benefit from these resources. I do not know what price is paid, probably $40 or $50 per ton for this crude steel, whereas it would be worth several hundred dollars per ton in finished form. In Nova Scotia and Cape Breton there is a large surplus of labour. Many of the younger people have not been able to get employment. If these crude iron materials were processed in our locality, it would give a great volume of employment.
In any event, it is a fact that the large portion of this material has been shipped away during the war years and since, so I suppose we have to be thankful for what has been done. I should like to ask the minister if he has any misgivings as to the importation of steel into Canada, owing to cheaper labour and depreciated currency in European countries? That would make it difficult for our own steel and iron companies to compete with these importations from Europe. I .feel the European industry has now reached the point where it is about to menace the manufacturers in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, there is no indication at present that Canadian industry is not well able to compete with European competition. Dosco has no difficulty competing with British steels in the British Columbia market, and that has always been a competitive area for the Canadian steel industry. Dosco has taken several orders away from European competition entirely on a price basis. The prices quoted are the Canadian f.o.b. price plus the water freight from Dosco to the west coast. The reason we have been cutting down
Supply-Trade and Commerce the subsidies, and plan to do away with them entirely at the end of this fiscal year, is that conditions are coming back to normal. For some years it was impossible to ship by water freight owing to the scarcity of tonnage and high freight rates. Today freight rates are back to normal, and there is ample tonnage. The markets that were normal markets for Dosco are opening up under conditions similar to those prevailing before the war. We feel that we have bridged over the transition period and allowed the steel plants to function as they did in pre-war days.
Can the minister say where the steel for the pipe line came from in British Columbia? That was something that was brought out in the committee.
The pipe line from where?
The oil pipe line.
From Alberta to the lakehead?
Yes.

All the 16-inch pipe was made in Welland of Canadian steel. Unfortunately that is the upper limit of capacity for the plant and therefore the 20-inch pipe had to be bought in the United States or fabricated in the United States, although all the steel plate that Canadian manufacturers could supply was made in Canada and shipped over to the United States for that purpose.

Is that for the portion of the
pipe line which is laid in the states as well or only for the portion laid in Canada?
No, the portion that is laid in Canada.

I should like to
ask the minister whether, if the subsidy that was paid for transporting steel from Nova Scotia could have been applied toward the processing of that steel in Nova Scotia instead of shipping it to steel plants and other plants in central Canada, it would not have resulted in building up those processing plants in Nova Scotia. I understand that a considerable portion of the subsidy was paid to transport this material from Nova Scotia to central Canada to be processed there rather than in. Nova Scotia. The question I ask is this, and I repeat it. Could not that subsidy be applied towards assisting in the erection of plants in Nova Scotia to do the processing and thus avoid shipping this raw material to; central Canada?

.Up until a few months ago this subsidy was applied to the shipping of finished steel from Dosco into central Canada. In other words, when conditions were abnormal we changed the geography of Canada to the extent of placing the Dosco plant in Montreal

Supply-Trade and Commerce as far as marketing in Canada was concerned. We absorbed the freight rate on the finished product between Sydney and Montreal. As I say, that procedure has been discontinued for the reason that distribution of finished material is taking its normal pattern now. The distribution of semi-finished steel from Dosco to plants owned by Dosco in other parts of Canada has been discontinued. The only subsidies that are now being paid are on semi-finished materials that Dosco are not able to finish, for the reason that they have not the capacity to do so; that material includes certain slabs, billets and certain pig iron that are surplus to their finishing capacity. We pay a subvention on that material to transport it to plants under different ownership who have surplus finishing capacity, and allow it to be converted there and to be put into channels of trade without raising the price of other materials being converted in the same plants.
As I understand, large payments were made in the way of subsidy to bring a considerable tonnage from Nova Scotia as far as Hamilton so that it could be processed there.
A fair tonnage, yes.

I was asking why the subsidy could not apply to encouraging the establishing of processing plants in Nova Scotia-we have suffered from that situation for years and years-rather than be a subsidy to move the raw material as far as Hamilton, for refining and processing there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Carried.

No. I
should like to ask a question.
I should like to get an answer.

Of course a good deal of the company's money and a good deal of the government's money was spent in enlarging the facilities in Nova Scotia both for primary steel and for finished steel. A good many mills were enlarged. New blast furnaces were installed. Just how far that procedure can go is limited by the profitable markets that can be found for the finished steel in normal times. That is a matter for the management to decide. I do not think any government can decide that. But we were simply taking care of the transition from a state of war to a state of normal distribution in the steel industry.

Following the question asked by the hon. member for Cumberland, may I ask if it is not true that during the last war the coal industry, the steel industry, in fact the whole Sydney situation, to some extent suffered because of the, let us say, strategic necessity? At any rate, they did not derive the same benefits as did central Canada from the development they had. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke about a fertilizer plant coming to an end during the war. Is that correct?
No fertilizer plant that I know of came to upper Canada from Nova Scotia during the war.
No, not during the war. It was quite a long time before the war.
When I was still a boy, I think.

No, not as
long ago as that. I was there when it was working.

The minister has been given some new powers. Not all of us helped him to get them, but he has them at any rate; and we are later running into the situation where in spite of ourselves the government is going to have influence on development. It seems to me that it would be a proper thing to bear in mind the needs of the east coast as suggested by the hon. member for Cumberland.

I can assure all hon. members that the government will go much further in developing industry in the less industrialized areas than it will in the industrialized areas. We have done things for industry in the maritime provinces and for industry in the prairie provinces that we would not think of doing for the same industry in Ontario or Quebec.

The minister spoke of blast furnace capacity. Has he any information or any estimate of what the increase in blast furnace capacity in the 'basic steel industry is likely to be in the next year or two?
I think there is another 800 tons a day going up at the moment.
Where? At Hamilton?
In Hamilton.
And at the Soo?
No new blast furnace capacity at the Soo; new finishing capacity at the Soo.
